rows.verified: A competent person must inspect excavation supports or battering at the start of the working shift and at specified times.
Work must not proceed until the excavation is safe.
Planning information should include ground conditions, underground structures, watercourses and existing services.
Excavations must not undermine scaffold footings, buried services or nearby foundations and walls.
Underground services must be identified and injury risks controlled before excavation starts.
Water inflow and additional water loading must be considered in the design of excavation support and dewatering.
Safe access and egress must be provided, with ladders secured and suitably extended where used.
Excavations must be re-inspected after events that could affect stability, and faults must be corrected immediately.
Excavation risk depends on soil, depth, support, water, nearby structures, buried services, plant, weather and inspection quality.
HSE excavation guidance is ground-, structure-, service-, plant-, worker-, control- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level collapse probability.
Commercial demolition clients must appoint designers and contractors with suitable skills, knowledge and experience.
Clients and principal designers must provide relevant pre-construction information.
Principal designers plan and manage health and safety during the pre-construction phase.
Principal contractors plan and manage health and safety during demolition.
Site managers must supervise workers and enforce safe working practices.
Demolition methods must control structural stability and the build-up and spread of debris.
Plans should define safe working zones, exclusion zones and debris zones.
Dutyholders must protect workers and the public from collapse, work-at-height, dust, debris and other demolition risks.
Demolition risk depends on structure, sequence, method, temporary stability, adjacent property, exclusion zones, plant and competent supervision.
HSE demolition guidance is structure-, method-, contractor-, site-, public-interface- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level collapse probability.
Chainsaws can cause fatal or major injuries when they are not used correctly.
Anyone using a chainsaw at work must receive adequate training relevant to the work undertaken.
Chainsaw operators must be competent for the type of chainsaw work they perform.
Operators are required to wear appropriate chainsaw protective clothing.
Safe chainsaw management includes fitness to operate, selection, maintenance, PPE and first-aid arrangements.
Tree felling and off-ground chainsaw work require task-specific competence and controls.
Lone-working arrangements must be considered for chainsaw work.
HSE investigations identify shortcuts and failure to follow good practice as common factors in fatal and major injuries.
Chainsaw risk depends on task, tree, terrain, saw condition, competence, PPE, weather, public access and emergency rescue arrangements.
HSE chainsaw guidance is operator-, equipment-, tree-, terrain-, control- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level injury probability.
